_守住的数字: p29–p30 转入后半：**How to do (deep RL) research**。开场先放一句 **Preface: A diversity of research approaches is good.**

⚠ 讲者的自我限定（和前半那句 not exhaustive 对称）：**「there's many different ways to do research… if everyone did research the exact way that I do research, then we would probably have fewer diverse discoveries. And so diversity is good. And my research approach is not necessarily the best approach.」**

p31 **Backstory**：**I had no intention to have a career in research.（You don't either!）** · 原本打算去工业界做产品（父母就是各种工程领域的）· 实习后发现自己对 AI 和算法开发感兴趣，而**那个前沿在研究环境里而不在工业界** · **Wanted to work on the frontier of AI research, on topics that weren't ready / didn't work yet.** · **The people I met working on those topics in industry all had PhDs.** · **Found ambiguity of research to be intellectually stimulating.**

⚠⚠ p32 **Some Realities** 三条：**1. Less than 1% of research ideas have lasting impact.**（**Many ideas don't lead to papers. Many papers have small impact.**）· **2. Research is incremental.** · **3. In a world where scale is important, simple ideas have more impact because they can be scaled**
⇒ 第 2 条的例子：**AlphaFold** —— **Builds closely on large 20-year academic project, CASP (critical assessment of structure prediction), and advances in neural networks.**
⇒ 讲者补了一句关于「失败的用处」：即使某个项目不是突破，**它也让别人能在上面接着做，或者让别人能排除掉已经试过的想法**
⇒ 第 3 条的理由：**简单的想法才是能 scale 的、容易被集成进不同系统的、容易在上面接着做的**
p33 大纲（**first three are equally important!**）：**1. What to work on · 2. How to do the work · 3. How to share the work · 4. Misc**
⚠⚠ p34–p36 **挑什么做的三步法**。**Need two things: (1) an important problem (2) a plan for how to approach it**
⇒ 两个反例把这件事钉住了：**Solve climate change ← I'm missing (2)**（重要但没路子）· **A really cool algorithm that will make the robot 1% more successful ← I'm missing (1)**（有路子但问题不重要）

⇒ **Step 1: What will the outcome look like if you are very successful?** —— 讲稿的说法是看**上限**：「**what is the upper bound of that project? And if the upper bound is not very high, then usually it doesn't make for a very good project**」
⇒ **Step 2: Are you excited about it?** —— **Research is a ton of work. You will be far more successful if you are excited.**
⚠ **Step 3: If you are brutally honest about why it could fail to solve the problem, does the idea still have high chance of working? If not, it probably won't work.**

⚠⚠ p37 **Problem-driven research vs. Idea-driven research**。**从想法出发**：你得去找一个它能解的问题，而 **There may not exist an important problem that the idea solves!**；目标是 **get the idea to work**。**从问题出发**：你去找最好的解法；坏处是 **May be harder to write paper if solution is obvious in retrospect**，但 **guaranteed to be working on an important problem :)**；目标是 **solve the problem**
⇒ 讲者自己的倾向与理由：从想法出发时，**就算它能解某个问题，也可能存在更好的解法 —— 那这个想法就没多少影响力**；而且「the second camp seems like a much more comfortable place to be because **it's possible that the idea just doesn't want to work**」
p38 **Bottlenecks** —— 讲稿：**如果问题卡在数据上，而你去研究算法，那你多半看不到性能提升**（「maybe you'll see a couple percentage points because really the big performance gains are going to be on the data side」）
⇒ 而这招也可以用在很长远的目标上：想让 LLM 证明人类没证过的东西、想让机器人在陌生厨房里做一碗麦片 —— **这些单个项目都解不了，但你可以问「到那里的瓶颈是什么」，然后在下一个项目里做那一段**

⚠⚠ p39 **那个「别把自己框在一个领域里」的故事**：博士第二年在 Google 实习，想用机器人做点酷的，计划是**建一个预测模型（视频生成）来跨机器人学技能**。**Problem: I discovered that existing video generation models were really bad** —— 当时最好的模型**把视频里的物体全擦掉了、几乎没抓住手臂的运动、连背景都没弄对**

⇒ **I am a ML+robotics person, not a computer vision person.** 但她**Decided to work on first developing a better video generation model!** —— 而且承认自己**不是做这件事最合适的人**（没建过生成模型、不太懂架构），只是**当时没多少人在做，因为大家没意识到这些模型有多差**
⇒ 结果：**resulting paper was basis for work in my job talk, has 1300 citations, and informed the community that it's an interesting problem to study** ⇒ **Takeaway: Don't box yourself into one area.**
p40 **Don't be a perfectionist.** · **You can never know a research project's impact at the outset.** · **Crossing topic boundaries informs new problems and brings new ideas**

⚠⚠ p42 **Key consideration: handling risk** 四条：**1. Front-load the risk whenever possible**（**a. Before developing large-scale infrastructure, formulate and run didactic experiments that test core unknowns**）· **2. Design targeted experiments that test unknowns in fastest possible way** · **3. Try out lots of ideas, including different problems — "create luck"** · **4. Don't mentally commit to project before signs of life on core unknown**
⇒ 旁注两句：**Lots of tricks, not all of them apply to all scenarios** · **This is uncomfortable!!** · 并回指 **Recall: Less than 1% of research ideas have lasting impact.**
⇒ 为什么「不舒服」：讲稿说**搭基础设施、把算法写出来，那常常是容易的部分，也是看起来在进步的部分**；而你要是先做完这些、最后才发现核心未知数不成立，**那些时间全白费了 —— 虽然当时看起来像在进步**

⚠ 两个把风险前置的**具体例子**（只在讲稿里）：① 元学习 —— 真要在机器人上搭一套元学习系统工作量巨大，于是她先把任务换成**回归一维正弦曲线**，测「能不能用五个数据点学会拟合」，**一天就写完了**，结果不错，才接着做；② 近期做让机器人听不同策略的语言指令 —— 两个风险里**「让机器人真的注意到不同策略」是更大的那个**，于是她找了一个数据集，**有些数据机器人用右手、有些用左手**，训个策略只看它能不能做到这件极简的事，**而且左右手可以从数据里自动判定、不用标注**

⚠⚠ p43 **Getting things to work** 五条：**1. Start from something that works and then make it incrementally harder** · **2. Simplify** · **3. Talk to friends, colleagues, advisers** · **4. Revisit your assumptions - some of the things you thought to be true at the beginning of the project may be refuted by your experiments** · **5. Does it "want" to work?**（**a. If not at all, then likely won't be impactful** · **b. Can you reduce the project scope to the parts that "want" to work?**）
⇒ 第 1/2 条的故事：想让机器人**看人做一遍再自己做**，采了很多样的机器人示范再请人照着做，**而且告诉采数据的人「随便做、多做些」**。结果 **nothing worked**，**花了几个月**。于是简化到**单任务** —— **结果连单任务也不行**，调通之后才 **1 个任务 → 3 个 → 10 个**

⇒ 第 5 条的故事：做让机器人听开放式语言指令（**Can you clean up the trash but not the dishes?**），**初步有苗头**；然后又加上「指令含糊时让机器人反问」等一堆想法，**things weren't really working，又花了几个月**。最后回头问「哪些部分是真的能跑的」，**把不会跑的那些砍掉、只保留方法本来就能处理的交互，砍掉的部分写成论文的 limitations**

⚠⚠ p44 **Deciding when to pivot**。**Often considered later than it should be considered!** · **"sunk cost fallacy"** · 原本的决策形式 **"continue working on current project" vs. "switch to starting a new project"** 而 **This is a super nebulous thing!**

⇒ 解法是**换一个问法**：**Advice: spend time thinking about other research projects!** ⇒ 把决策改成 **"continue working on current project" vs. "work on project B" vs. "work on project C" vs. …** ⇒ **This decision is a lot more straightforward, less anxiety inducing! 🥳**
⇒ 沉没成本那条讲稿说得更准：**人很自然会想「我在这上面花了很多时间，所以以后花的时间会更少」—— 这是谬误，而且你实际的进展可能配不上你花掉的时间**
⚠ 课堂提问（关于**被抢发**）：讲者的回答是 —— 抢先做某个想法确实有优势，**但把一个项目执行得很好也有很大优势，而且被执行得更好的项目常常比「第一个提出那个想法」的项目更有影响力**；所以她的建议仍然是**在执行与评估上花足够的功夫**

notes.t: 三条现实：不到 1% 有持久影响、研究是增量的、简单想法影响更大
notes.quote:
How to do (deep RL) research
Preface: A diversity of research approaches is good.
Backstory: I had no intention to have a career in research. (You don't either!) · Wanted to work on the frontier of AI research, on topics that weren't ready / didn't work yet. · The people I met working on those topics in industry all had PhDs. · Found ambiguity of research to be intellectually stimulating.
Some Realities
1. Less than 1% of research ideas have lasting impact. — Many ideas don't lead to papers. Many papers have small impact.
2. Research is incremental. — Example: Builds closely on large 20-year academic project, CASP (critical assessment of structure prediction), and advances in neural networks.
3. In a world where scale is important, simple ideas have more impact because they can be scaled
Outline: 1. What to work on · 2. How to do the work · 3. How to share the work · 4. Misc  ← first three are equally important!

And so diversity is good. And my research approach is not necessarily the best approach」。
⇒ 所以这 25 页的正确读法是：一位高产研究者的个人工作方式，而不是一套必须照做的规程。 ⇒ 和前半那句 this will not be exhaustive 配着看，这位讲者在两处都先声明了自己的局限 —— 这本身就是一种可以学的习惯。
p31 的 Backstory 有一句很解压的话：I had no intention to have a career in research. (You don't either!) 原本的打算是去工业界做产品（她父母就在各种工程领域做这个），觉得那才是「有真实世界影响」的路。实习之后发现自己对 AI 和算法开发感兴趣，而那个前沿在研究环境里而不在工业界。

⇒ 她当时想做的东西，幻灯写得很准：topics that weren't ready / didn't work yet（还没成熟、还跑不通的题目）。而推动她读博的理由很实在：The people I met working on those topics in industry all had PhDs. ⇒ 第三条理由是性格上的：Found ambiguity of research to be intellectually stimulating —— 研究的「说不清」本身是一种吸引力，而不是要克服的障碍。

⚠️ p32 的三条现实是这几页的核心，而第一条最硬：Less than 1% of research ideas have lasting impact. 幻灯把这件事分成两层：Many ideas don't lead to papers（很多想法连论文都变不成）＋ Many papers have small impact（变成了论文的也多半影响很小）。⇒ 讲稿里她直接放了自己一堆想法的结局：「here are the outcomes of some of my research ideas. And here are the outcome of some more of my research ideas. And there's a lot of failure」。
⇒ 而这一条不是用来打击人的，它是后面整套方法论的前提：讲稿说「a lot of what I'll say has to do with dealing with that sort of risk」。 ⇒ 换句话说：p42 那套「把风险前置、多试、不要早早承诺」，之所以是对的，正是因为这个 1%。⇒ 读这几页时要把两处连起来，否则 p42 看起来只是一堆技巧。

第二条：Research is incremental.而例子选得很有分量 —— AlphaFold。 幻灯的说明：Builds closely on large 20-year academic project, CASP (critical assessment of structure prediction), and advances in neural networks。⇒ 一个被广泛当成「突破」的成果，自己也是增量的：它站在一个二十年的学术项目（提供了竞赛与数据集）和神经网络的进展上。
⇒ 讲者还顺手给了「失败也有用」一个具体的理由，而不是安慰话：即使某个项目不是突破，它也让别人能在上面接着做，或者让别人能排除掉已经试过的想法。 ⇒ 后半句尤其实在：「这条路我们试过了，不行」本身是一个对社群有价值的产出——而这也接到了 p46 那句「就算效果不好也值得分享」。
⚠️ 第三条最反直觉，而且它是一条选题判据：In a world where scale is important, simple ideas have more impact because they can be scaled。 讲稿的理由有三层：简单的想法能被放大、容易被集成进不同的系统、容易让别人在上面接着做。

⇒ 这条的实际含义是：「我的算法很精巧」常常是一个缺点而不是优点。 ⇒ 一个需要五个超参、三个阶段、两个辅助损失才能跑的方法，即使它在你的实验里更好，也很难被别人用上——而影响力来自被用上。⇒ 讲稿的原话是「oftentimes it's actually the simple ideas that have more impact than the fancy ideas or the complex algorithms」。

p33 的大纲有一个容易被跳过、却是讲者刻意强调的旁注：first three are equally important! 三件事是：① 挑什么做 ② 怎么做 ③ 怎么分享。而讲稿把这个强调的用意说明了：「it's easy to think that maybe number 2 is the most important or maybe number 1. But all of these are actually really, really important」。
⇒ 这个排序值得想一下，因为大多数人（尤其是工程背景的人）会默认 ② 最重要。 ⇒ 而讲者把 ③ 提到同等地位的理由在 p46：研究的产出是知识，知识没人知道就等于没有产出。⇒ 所以这不是「也要注意宣传」，而是「不分享 = 没做」。

notes.say:
原话（我的方法不一定是最好的）：“I'll talk a lot about how I go about the research process and advice that I give to PhD students… But there's many different ways to do research. And it's important and good for the community to do research in many different ways because that leads to more diverse discoveries. And if everyone did research the exact way that I do research, then we would probably have fewer diverse discoveries. And so diversity is good. And my research approach is not necessarily the best approach. And I don't think there's any one approach that is the best approach.”

原话（不到 1%，而这是后面整套方法论的前提）：“The first is that very, very few research ideas are good. And very, very few research ideas have impact, have lasting impact especially. A lot of ideas don't work. A lot of ideas don't work to the extent that they won't lead to papers. As an example of this, here are the outcomes of some of my research ideas. And here are the outcome of some more of my research ideas. And there's a lot of failure. And the risk and the challenge of doing research informs different ways—— a lot of what I'll say has to do with dealing with that sort of risk and dealing with those challenges.”

原话（AlphaFold 也是增量的；而失败的具体用处）：“AlphaFold, arguably like a really impactful thing, very, very successful, arguably could be considered a breakthrough. This itself was, in many ways, incremental. It built very closely on a large 20-year academic project called CASP… and also built very heavily on advances in neural networks. And so even if any one research project isn't a breakthrough, it often plays an important role because it allows other projects to build on it or other projects to potentially rule out ideas that have been tried already.”

原话（为什么简单的想法影响更大）：“oftentimes people think about developing really cool, fancy algorithms. But in a world where scaling up is often quite important, especially in AI research, oftentimes it's actually the simple ideas that have more impact than the fancy ideas or the complex algorithms. And that's just because the simple ideas are the things that can scale, that are the things that are easy to be integrated into different systems, and easy to build on top of.”

res.v:
⚠️ 第三条现实（简单想法影响更大，因为只有简单的东西能被 scale）对你是一条直接可用的辩护，而且它正好回应了一个你很可能会收到的质疑。
那个质疑长这样：「你的方法很简单啊 —— 不就是 G = Acc − λ·Cost 加一个节点级的档位选择？新颖性在哪？」
⇒ 按这一页，正确的回答不是去把方法变复杂，而是把简单当成设计目标说出来：我们的目标函数只有一个系数、我们的决策是逐节点的二选一、我们的第二阶段是一个标准的监督回归 —— 这些都是刻意的，因为只有这样它才能被接到别人的工作流上。⇒ 而这件事是可以证明的，不只是声称：在论文里给出「把我们的方法接到一个新工作流上需要改什么」的清单。如果那个清单只有两三行，那就是「可 scale」的实证。
⚠ 而第一条现实（不到 1%）对你有一个更要紧的含义，它关系到你现在该怎么安排时间。
讲者明说这一条是后面整套方法论的前提：「a lot of what I'll say has to do with dealing with that sort of risk」。⇒ 也就是说，p42 那套做法不是「良好习惯」，而是对这个基础概率的理性反应。
⇒ 对你最具体的一条：你的核心未知数是「节点级到底比工作流级好多少」，而这件事现在还没有答案。⇒ 按这一页的逻辑，在这个数出来之前，你不该把时间花在搭完整的搜索框架上 —— 那正是 p42 要防的「看起来在进步，其实在赌」。⇒ 而这条和 L17 p29 那个消融（「只在第一个节点决定一次 vs 逐节点」）是同一件事：那个消融就是你的核心未知数，而它应该是你的第一个实验，不是最后一个。
⇒ 第二条现实（研究是增量的，AlphaFold 也站在 CASP 二十年之上）对你是一条措辞上的建议：不要试图把你的工作写成横空出世。 ⇒ 你的工作明确地站在三样东西上：AFlow 的工作流搜索、级联／路由那条线、以及分布无关的统计工具。把这三条血脉写清楚，比暗示自己什么都没依赖要可信得多，而且这正是 AlphaFold 那个例子要说的。
⚠ 最后那句「失败也有用 —— 让别人能排除掉已经试过的想法」对你有一个很实际的用处：你试过但没用的那些特征、那些档位策略，值得写进论文。 ⇒ 比如「我们试过用 logprob 当置信度特征，但因为校准问题（见 p22）它没有用」 —— 这一句话既是一个负面结果，也是一条让别人省时间的信息，而且它让审稿人看到你确实探过这个空间。⇒ 一个「我们试过什么、为什么不行」的小节，常常是审稿人最愿意相信的那一节。

notes.t: 挑什么做：三步法，和问题驱动 vs 想法驱动
notes.quote:
What to work on
Need two things: (1) an important problem (2) a plan for how to approach it
Examples: Solve climate change ← I'm missing (2)  ·  A really cool algorithm that will make the robot 1% more successful ← I'm missing (1)
Step 1: What will the outcome look like if you are very successful?
Step 2: Are you excited about it? — Research is a ton of work. You will be far more successful if you are excited.
Step 3: If you are brutally honest about why it could fail to solve the problem, does the idea still have high chance of working? If not, it probably won't work.
Problem-driven research vs. Idea-driven research
If you start with an idea, you need to find a problem. There may not exist an important problem that the idea solves! — Goal: get the idea to work
Starting with the problem, you try to find the best solution. May be harder to write paper if solution is obvious in retrospect. But guaranteed to be working on an important problem :) — Goal: solve the problem
notes.one: 一个项目要同时有「重要的问题」和「接近它的路子」。两个反例把这件事钉死了：解决气候变化缺路子，让机器人成功率涨 1% 的精巧算法缺问题。
pts: 核心主张就一行：Need two things: (1) an important problem (2) a plan for how to approach it，而讲者补了一句把它变成判据的话：只有一个的话，通常不构成一个好方向。
⇒ 两个反例选得很妙，因为它们一个缺这个、一个缺那个。Solve climate change —— 非常重要，但我没有路子（I'm missing (2)）。 ⇒ 这类方向的特征是：你说出来所有人都点头，但你明天不知道该写哪一行代码。
⇒ 另一个是 A really cool algorithm that will make the robot 1% more successful —— 有路子（甚至有两条），但缺一个它真正在解的重要问题（I'm missing (1)）。 ⚠ 注意幻灯刻意写了 1%：它不是说这个算法没用，而是说它的天花板太低。

⚠️ ⇒ 而 Step 1 就是用来检查这个天花板的：What will the outcome look like if you are very successful? 讲稿把它说成一个更锋利的问题：「what is the upper bound of that project? And if the upper bound is not very high, then usually it doesn't make for a very good project」。
⇒ 这个检查方式的好处是它在动手之前就能做，而且只需要诚实：假设一切顺利、实验全部成功，那时候的结论是什么？那个结论重要吗？ ⇒ 如果「一切顺利」的结局是「某个指标涨了 1%」，那不管过程多漂亮，上限就是 1%。

Step 2 是一条看起来软、其实很实用的检查：Are you excited about it? 理由幻灯写了：Research is a ton of work. You will be far more successful if you are excited.；讲稿还补了一句「this is actually probably true for a lot of things outside of research too」。

⇒ 它为什么是判据而不只是鼓励？因为它和第一条现实（不到 1%）是配套的：既然多数想法会失败，那你需要的是能撑过失败的动力。 ⇒ 讲稿的链条很清楚：「if it's fun… you're more likely to work hard on it. And if you're working hard on it, you're much more likely to be successful」。

⚠️ Step 3 是三步里最硬的一条，而且它的措辞要逐字读：If you are brutally honest about why it could fail to solve the problem, does the idea still have high chance of working? ⇒ 注意它不是问「这个想法有多大机会成」，而是问「把所有你能想到的失败理由摆上桌之后，它还有多大机会成」。
⇒ 幻灯的结论很干脆：If not, it probably won't work. 而讲稿给的理由又回到那个 1%：「that's mostly just because of the reality of most ideas not actually working in research」。 ⇒ 换句话说：基础概率已经很低了，所以你不该在还有已知的大风险时就乐观。
⚠️ p37 的 问题驱动 vs 想法驱动 是这几页最值得反复想的一页，而讲者明确说了自己偏向哪一边。 从想法出发：你手上有个漂亮的想法，然后去找一个它能解的问题。⇒ 风险是 There may not exist an important problem that the idea solves!

⇒ 而讲者补的那层更尖，也更容易被忽略：就算它确实解了某个问题，也可能存在更好的解法 —— 那这个想法就没多少影响力。 原话：「It may solve a problem. But there might be a better way to solve the problem. And if there's a better way to solve the problem, then that idea may not have a lot of impact」。
⇒ 从问题出发：你认定一个问题，然后去找最好的解法。坏处幻灯也写了：May be harder to write paper if solution is obvious in retrospect。 ⇒ 但好处是一句带笑脸的话：But guaranteed to be working on an important problem :)
⚠️ ⇒ 而把两者的差别讲得最透的是那组目标的对比：想法驱动的目标是 get the idea to work（让这个想法成），问题驱动的目标是 solve the problem（把问题解掉）。
⇒ 为什么后者「舒服得多」？讲者的理由是一句很妙的话：「it's possible that the idea just doesn't want to work」。 ⇒ 如果你的目标是「让这个想法成」，而这个想法本质上就不想成，那你就被困住了——因为放弃想法等于项目失败。⇒ 而如果目标是「解掉问题」，换一个想法只是换一条路，项目还活着。
⇒ 讲稿还说她两种都做过（「I've done research that's more idea-driven. I've also done research that's more problem driven」），只是自己更偏向问题驱动。 ⇒ 这个诚实的措辞也值得学：她给的是一个有理由的偏好，而不是一条规矩。

notes.say:
原话（两个反例，以及「上限」这个检查）：“maybe one project idea is I want to solve climate change. That is an important problem. But I don't have a plan for how to approach it. So it doesn't make a good research project even though it's a really important problem. Second, maybe I have a really cool algorithm that at best will make a robot or a reinforcement learning system a little bit more successful. This is maybe a really cool idea. And maybe I have a plan. Maybe I have two. But I'm missing the important problem that this is actually solving. And so… it's really important to think about, if the project is really, really successful, what will the outcome look like? Does it solve an important problem? Or what is the upper bound of that project? And if the upper bound is not very high, then usually it doesn't make for a very good project.”

原话（Step 3：把失败理由摆上桌之后还剩多少机会）：“a lot of ideas don't work. And so it's really good to think about, if you are brutally honest about why your idea could fail to solve the problem, does the idea still have a good chance of working? And if not, then probably it won't work. And that's mostly just because of the reality of most ideas not actually working in research. And it's important to be honest with yourself about whether this will actually solve the problem or not.”

原话（为什么偏向问题驱动 —— 因为想法可能「不想成」）：“if you start with an idea, you need to find a problem that that idea solves. And there may not exist an important problem that the idea solves. It may solve a problem. But there might be a better way to solve the problem. And if there's a better way to solve the problem, then that idea may not have a lot of impact. On the contrary, if you start with a problem, then you're trying to find the best solution to that problem. And one downside is it may be harder to write a paper if the solution ends up being kind of obvious in retrospect. But at least you're guaranteed to be working on an important problem.… Another way to put this is that with idea-driven research, your goal is to get the idea to work. Whereas in the second case, your goal is to solve the problem. And the second camp seems like a much more comfortable place to be because it's possible that the idea just doesn't want to work.”

res.v:
这几页值得你当场拿自己的课题过一遍，而三步里你有两步很稳、一步需要补。
(1) 重要的问题 ✓ 有，而且 .b 那片已经给你找到了最好的措辞：p27 点名的「做出能排除坏模型的离线指标」。 再加上 agentic 工作流的推理成本是一个正在变贵的真问题。⇒ 这一条不用再论证。
(2) 接近它的路子 ✓ 有：两阶段训练（特权信息教、可观测特征用）＋ 分布无关的排除保证。 ⇒ 这也不是空的，因为 L17 那套 RMA 架构给了你一个已经在三个领域跑通过的模板。
⚠️ Step 1（上限检查）—— 这一步你需要当场算一个数，而且它可能不好看。
问法是：假设一切顺利，结论会是什么？⇒ 对你就是：节点级档位分配，最好能把成本降到全用大模型的百分之几、而 Acc 掉多少？
⇒ 这个数你现在就能估，而且不用跑实验：取你的工作流，手工标出「哪些节点换小模型肯定没事」，算一下那样的成本占比。⚠ 如果答案是「最多省 15%」，那按这一页的标准，你的上限就是 15%，而那可能不足以支撑一篇论文。⇒ 而如果答案是「某些工作流上能省 60%」，那上限就很健康。⇒ 无论哪种，先把这个数算出来 —— 它决定了你该不该继续，而成本是一个下午。
⇒ 而 1% 那个反例对你是一个具体的警示：如果你的结果最后是「G 提升了 1.2 个点」，那你就正好落在幻灯画的那个反例上。 ⇒ 所以你的主结果应当是一个量级上的东西（成本减半而 Acc 基本不掉），而不是一个小数点。⇒ 这也反过来提示你该选哪些工作流做实验：选那些「大模型用得最浪费」的，而不是选最常见的。
⚠️ Step 3（残酷诚实）—— 把你能想到的失败理由摆上桌，而我替你摆三条最该摆的：
① 节点级可能并不比工作流级好多少（L17 p29 那个消融要查的就是这个）；② 第一个节点没有历史可看，而工作流只有 3–8 个节点（L17.d p68 那条冷启动）；③ 搜索成本可能超过节省（见 L16 那条摊销曲线）。
⇒ 把这三条摆上桌之后，这个想法还成不成？我的判断是：成，但前提是 ① 的答案是正面的。⇒ 而这就把 Step 3 和 p42 接上了：① 是你的核心未知数，所以它必须是第一个实验。
⇒ 最后，p37 那个对比给了你一个关于怎么写的判断：你是问题驱动的，所以你会吃到那个已知的坏处 ——「解法事后看显然，论文难写」。 ⇒ 这不是假设：「贵的节点用大模型、便宜的用小模型」事后看非常显然。⇒ 应对办法不是把方法写复杂，而是把「显然」的那部分做成基线，然后证明它不够：手工规则 / 全大 / 全小 / 按节点类型的固定映射，各是一条基线。⇒ 如果你的学出来的策略明显赢过这些「显然」的做法，那「显然」就成了你的论据而不是你的问题。

notes.quote:
What to work on — Bottlenecks
A couple more things.  ·  Year 2 of my PhD: internship
Build predictive model and use it to learn skills across many robots
Problem: I discovered that existing video generation models were really bad — ground truth / generation
I am a ML+robotics person, not a computer vision person.

notes.one: 两条：一是动手前先问「这个问题到底卡在哪」——卡在数据上就别去调算法；二是那个故事：她为了用上视频生成模型，先去把视频生成模型做好了，而她本来不做视觉。
pts: ⚠️ 瓶颈这一条虽然幻灯上只有一个词，但讲稿把它讲成了选题里最实用的一招：如果问题卡在数据上，而你去研究算法，那你多半看不到性能提升。 原话：「if the problem is bottlenecked on data, for example, and you start exploring new algorithms separate from the data… you actually probably won't see performance gains… maybe you'll see a couple percentage points because really, the big performance gains are going to be on the data side」。

⇒ 这一条和 Step 1（上限检查）其实是同一件事的两种问法：「上限有多高」问的是终点，「瓶颈在哪」问的是为什么现在到不了终点。 ⇒ 而后者更可操作，因为它直接告诉你该动哪里。⇒ 讲者的总结：「a lot of problem-driven research ends up thinking about what is the bottleneck for solving this problem」。
⇒ 而这一招还能用在很长远的目标上，这是讲稿里最漂亮的一段用法。 她举的两个例子都大得不像研究项目：让 LLM 证明人类没证过的东西（比如 P vs NP）、让机器人在一个陌生厨房里做一碗麦片。

⇒ 用法是：这些单个项目都解不了，但你可以问「到那里的瓶颈是什么」，然后在下一个项目里做那一段。 原话：「you can think about, OK, what's the bottleneck for getting there? And can I work on the part of that problem in my next project that will make progress on that larger goal?」⇒ 这就把「宏大目标」从空话变成了一个可执行的分解方式 —— 它不是让你放弃宏大目标，而是让你用它来挑下一步。
⚠️ p39 那个故事是整讲最具体的一个，而且它的每一步都值得记。 博士第二年在 Google 实习，那里有一堆机器人，她想用它们做点酷的。计划：建一个预测模型（视频生成模型），用它跨机器人学技能。

⇒ 然后撞上了问题，而幻灯写得很平静：Problem: I discovered that existing video generation models were really bad。 有多差？讲稿描述了那张对比图：当时最好的视频生成模型「is erasing all the objects in the video and is barely capturing the motion of the arm. Doesn't even capture the background correctly」。⇒ 于是她的原计划做不下去了。

⚠️ ⇒ 这里是分叉点，而幻灯把她当时的自我认知写了出来：I am a ML+robotics person, not a computer vision person. 讲稿补了那个本来很自然的选择：「If I kind of felt like I should only work on machine learning and robotics, I might have to table this and figure out a different project」。

⇒ 但她的决定是：Decided to work on first developing a better video generation model! ⚠ 而讲稿里那段自我评估很诚实，也很重要：「arguably, I wasn't necessarily the best person to do this. I had never built a generative model before. I didn't really know that much about architectures for doing so」。

⇒ 那她凭什么能做成？理由只有一条，而且是结构性的：「not a lot of people were working on it at the time because they didn't realize how bad these models were」。 ⇒ 这一句是整个故事的机制：她之所以有机会，正是因为她从另一个方向走过来、因而看到了别人看不到的问题。⇒ 做视觉的人不知道这些模型在机器人上有多不够用，因为他们不拿它做控制。
⇒ 结果：那篇论文成了她 job talk 的基础、约 1300 次引用，而且让社群意识到这是一个值得研究的问题（后来别人做出了比她那个好得多的模型）。 ⇒ 注意最后那半句也被幻灯写进去了：「informed the community that it's an interesting problem to study」——把一个问题标记出来，本身是一种贡献。

⇒ Takeaway: Don't box yourself into one area. 而 p40 给了理由：Crossing topic boundaries informs new problems and brings new ideas。 讲稿把这个双向性说清楚了：你想用某个东西而它不好用 ⇒ 这件事本身就说明那个领域有个问题，而那个领域的人常常不知道；同时你也把新想法带进了那个领域。

p40 第二条是 Don't be a perfectionist.，理由是一句很干脆的话：You can never know a research project's impact at the outset. 讲稿加了半句把它变成了逻辑而不是鼓励：「Otherwise, it wouldn't be research」。⇒ 所以结论是：「挑一个完美的项目」这件事在定义上就做不到，于是你得在某个点上直接开始试。
⚠ 把这三页并起来，它们其实在反对同一种行为：在动手之前过度优化选择。 ⇒ 瓶颈那条说「别在错的地方使劲」，故事那条说「别因为领域标签就放弃一条路」，完美主义那条说「别为了选对而迟迟不开始」。⇒ 三条合起来的姿态是：想清楚该往哪使劲，然后尽快开始，并且不介意绕路。

notes.say:
原话（瓶颈：卡在数据上就别去调算法；以及怎么用它分解宏大目标）：“if you're thinking about a problem that you want to solve, it's really important to get to the bottleneck of that problem. So if the problem is bottlenecked on data, for example, and you start exploring new algorithms separate from the data for how to solve it, then you actually probably won't see performance gains from working on methods if it's bottlenecked by data. And most, maybe you'll see a couple percentage points because really, the big performance gains are going to be on the data side… You can think about, I want to develop an LLM that can prove something that humans have never proved before, like P versus NP or something. Or I want to get a robot that can make a bowl of cereal in a new kitchen. Those are things that you can't solve in any individual research project. But you can think about, OK, what's the bottleneck for getting there? And can I work on the part of that problem in my next project that will make progress on that larger goal?”

原话（那个故事，以及她为什么有机会）：“I discovered that video generation models were really bad. So here was a video that I collected on the robot. And here was a prediction from arguably the state of the art video generation model. And you can see that it is erasing all the objects in the video and is barely capturing the motion of the arm. Doesn't even capture the background correctly.… Now, at the time, I kind of viewed myself as a machine learning and robotics person and not really a computer vision person… If I kind of felt like I should only work on machine learning and robotics, I might have to table this and figure out a different project to work on. But instead, I decided to work on trying to develop a better video generation model. Now, arguably, I wasn't necessarily the best person to do this. I had never built a generative model before. I didn't really know that much about architectures for doing so. But not a lot of people were working on it at the time because they didn't realize how bad these models were. And then the resulting paper ended up being the basis for work in my job talk, now has around 1,300 citations. And it arguably informed the community that it's kind of an interesting problem to study.”

原话（别做完美主义者 —— 因为那在定义上做不到）：“I've seen people feel like they want to pick the perfect project to work on. But you never know what the impact of a project will be at the outset. Otherwise, it wouldn't be research. And so at some point, you need to just start trying different ideas, start getting going on a project without trying to find the perfect project.”

res.v:
⚠️ 「先找瓶颈」这一条，是这几页对你最该当场执行的一件事，因为你的课题有一个很可能被忽略的瓶颈。
讲者的判据是：如果问题卡在 X 上，而你在研究 Y，那你多半只能看到几个百分点。⇒ 那么你的问题到底卡在哪？
⇒ 至少有三个候选，而它们指向完全不同的工作：① 卡在「不知道哪个节点该降档」（＝一个预测问题，你现在做的就是这个）；② 卡在「搜索太贵」（＝一个计算问题，对应 L17.c p45 那条「把真跑挪出内循环」）；③ 卡在「小模型就是不行」（＝一个能力问题，那么任何路由都救不了）。
⇒ 而 ③ 是最该先排除的，因为如果它成立，①②都白做。 ⇒ 怎么排除？一个下午的实验：在你的工作流上，逐节点地把那一个节点换成小模型、其余全用大模型，量每个节点单独降档的 Acc 损失。⇒ 如果所有节点单独降档都掉很多，那小模型在这个工作流上就是不够用，瓶颈是能力，不是路由。⇒ 如果有一批节点单独降档几乎不掉，那路由就确实有空间，而且你顺手得到了空间的上界。
⇒ 注意这个实验同时回答了 Step 1 的「上限」问题（见 p34 的科研格）—— 两件事一个实验就办了，而这正是 p42「用最快的方式测未知数」的意思。
⚠️ 而 p39 那个故事对你有一条不太好听但很值得想的提醒：你的瓶颈可能不在你擅长的那一侧。
讲者本来是 ML+机器人的人，结果发现卡在视频生成上 —— 一个她不擅长、而且自认不是最合适的人去做的方向。而她的选择是去做那个。
⇒ 对你，这个对应可能是：你的验收标准里有「写 bound」，那是理论那一侧；而你的瓶颈可能在工程那一侧（搜索成本、评测管线），或者反过来。⇒ 诚实地判断一下：如果你把界写得很漂亮，但实验只能在一个工作流上跑，那篇论文站得住吗？反过来呢？⇒ 这一页的建议是按瓶颈分配时间，而不是按擅长分配时间。
⇒ 而那个故事的机制部分（她之所以有机会，是因为从另一个方向走过来、看到了别人看不到的问题）对你其实是有利的消息。 ⇒ 你在做的是 **把 bandit／统计那边的工具（分布无关的保证、实验设计）搬到 agentic LLM 工作流上**。⇒ 这正是一次跨界：做 agent 的人多半不知道有这些工具，做理论的人多半不知道这个问题。⇒ 而按这一页，这种位置恰恰是机会最大的位置 —— 而且它也解释了为什么你能在一个「有人在附近」的方向上仍然有空间。
⚠ 最后那句「把一个问题标记给社群，本身是一种贡献」给了你一个降低压力的选项：即使你的方法只是部分成功，把「节点级保真度分配」这个问题讲清楚、给出基线和难点，本身就有价值。 ⇒ 这不是退而求其次 —— 讲者那篇 1300 引用的论文，她自己说后来别人做出了比她好得多的模型。⇒ 她的贡献有一半在于「指出这里有个问题」。

notes.t: 怎么处理风险：把它前置、从能跑的东西出发、以及什么时候转向
notes.quote:
Key consideration: handling risk
1. Front-load the risk whenever possible — a. Before developing large-scale infrastructure, formulate and run didactic experiments that test core unknowns
2. Design targeted experiments that test unknowns in fastest possible way
3. Try out lots of ideas, including different problems — “create luck”
4. Don't mentally commit to project before signs of life on core unknown
Lots of tricks, not all of them apply to all scenarios · This is uncomfortable!! · Recall: Less than 1% of research ideas have lasting impact.
Getting things to work
1. Start from something that works and then make it incrementally harder · 2. Simplify · 3. Talk to friends, colleagues, advisers · 4. Revisit your assumptions - some of the things you thought to be true at the beginning of the project may be refuted by your experiments · 5. Does it “want” to work? — a. If not at all, then likely won't be impactful · b. Can you reduce the project scope to the parts that “want” to work?
Deciding when to pivot
Often considered later than it should be considered! · “sunk cost fallacy”
“continue working on current project” vs. “switch to starting a new project” — This is a super nebulous thing!
Advice: spend time thinking about other research projects!
“continue working on current project” vs. “work on project B” vs. “work on project C” vs. … — This decision is a lot more straightforward, less anxiety inducing! 🥳
notes.one: 三页技巧，但它们服务同一个数字：不到 1% 的想法有持久影响。所以别先搭基础设施——那是容易的部分，也是看起来在进步的部分；先用最快的办法去测那个核心未知数。
pts: ⚠️ 先把 p42 第 1 条读准，因为它反对的恰恰是最舒服的工作方式：Front-load the risk whenever possible —— Before developing large-scale infrastructure, formulate and run didactic experiments that test core unknowns。 didactic experiment 就是「教学玩具式的实验」：小、快、只为回答一个问题。

⇒ 而讲稿解释了为什么人们不这么做，这一段是整页最诚实的地方：搭基础设施、把算法写出来，常常是容易的部分，也是看起来在进步的那部分。 原话：「oftentimes, building the infrastructure, coding the algorithm, whatever, that's like the easy part. That's the part where you can seemingly make some progress」。

⇒ 后果说得很直接：「if you do all that and then, at the end, realize that the core unknown actually ended up not working out, then you wasted all of that time—— even though it seemingly seemed like progress」。 ⇒ 所以幻灯那句 This is uncomfortable!! 不是在说实验难做，而是在说「先去面对那个可能毁掉整个项目的问题」这件事本身让人不舒服。

第 2 条是第 1 条的技能版：Design targeted experiments that test unknowns in fastest possible way。 讲稿强调这是一项需要功夫的能力：「thinking through how to test ideas in the simplest possible way or the fastest possible way takes some skill and takes some thinking. It's often not obvious how to test a particular hypothesis」。
⚠️ ⇒ 而讲稿给了两个具体例子，这两个例子是这几页最值得照抄的东西（幻灯上没有）。 例一 · 元学习：目标是让机器人用很少的数据快速适应新任务。但在真机上搭一套元学习系统工作量巨大。⇒ 于是她把任务换成「回归一维正弦曲线」，只测「能不能用五个数据点学会拟合」——「it was this experiment that I coded up in a day」，结果不错，才接着做。
⇒ 例二 · 语言指令（近期）：目标是让机器人听不同策略的语言指令。两个风险是「拿到好的策略标签」和「让机器人真的注意到不同策略」，而后者是更大的那个。 ⇒ 她的做法：找一个数据集，有些数据机器人用右手、有些用左手，训个策略只看它能不能做到这件极简的事。⚠ 而最妙的一笔是：左右手可以从数据里自动判定，不用标注 —— 这样就把第二个风险（标签）也绕开了，只留下她要测的那一个。
⇒ 两个例子的共同形状值得抽出来：把真实任务换成一个保留了核心未知数、但去掉了全部工程量的玩具任务。 ⇒ 正弦曲线保留了「少样本快速适应」，去掉了机器人；左右手保留了「策略能不能被语言区分」，去掉了标注和复杂指令。

第 3 条换了一个维度：Try out lots of ideas, including different problems — "create luck"。 讲稿的逻辑很清楚：「you have to get lucky to stumble upon a good idea. But you can create luck for yourself just by trying out lots of ideas」。⇒ 注意 including different problems 这半句 —— 不只是换想法，还可以换问题，因为「even at the outset, you don't know how hard a problem is going to be」。

⇒ 而她自己的经验写得很实在，包括没做到的时候：「there was kind of lots of times in my PhD where I tried out lots of ideas that didn't make it into papers. They failed… I didn't always do this. Sometimes, I ended up banging my head against the wall plenty of times」。
第 4 条是前三条的收口：Don't mentally commit to project before signs of life on core unknown。 ⇒ 关键词是 mentally（心理上）和 signs of life（有活的迹象）。⇒ 也就是说：在那个核心未知数给出正面信号之前，别让自己在心理上认定「这就是我的项目」——因为那之后你就很难放手了。

⚠️ p43 换到「已经动手了、但跑不通」这个场景，而第 1/2 条是其中最有用的：Start from something that works and then make it incrementally harder ＋ Simplify。 讲稿的理由：「if you coded up a system and it's not working, there's a million reasons that could be why… it's much easier to start with something that works and then make it harder than to start with something that doesn't work and try to get it to work」。
⇒ 而配的那个故事很能说明问题，而且有一个很关键的转折。 目标是让机器人看人做一遍再自己做。他们采了很多样的机器人示范，再请人照着做一遍，而且告诉采数据的人「随便做、多做些」。结果 nothing worked，花了几个月。

⚠️ ⇒ 转折在这里：他们简化到单任务去验证模仿学习这一套对不对 —— 结果连单任务也不行。 原话：「we simplified to just a single task setting. Like, can we get the robot to do one task and make sure our imitation learning stack works? It actually didn't work. And so we had to debug that, get it to work on one task, then get it to work on three tasks, then get it to work on 10 tasks」。
⇒ 这个转折是整个故事的要点：他们花了几个月在一个多任务问题上，而真正的毛病在最基础的那一层。 ⇒ 如果一开始就先跑通单任务，那几个月就省下来了。⇒ 所以「简化」不只是调试手段，它是一个定序原则：先确认地基，再往上加。

p43 第 4 条值得单独留意：Revisit your assumptions - some of the things you thought to be true at the beginning of the project may be refuted by your experiments。 讲稿的追问很到位：「has anything changed about my assumptions from the beginning? And then if something has changed, would that change the way that you're going about the project or even the project that you're working on?」

⚠️ 第 5 条「Does it "want" to work?」是 p43 最特别的一条，而它有两级。 a. 如果完全不想成，那它很可能没什么影响力 ——「if someone else is trying to get it to work and it also doesn't really work for them, then maybe the idea just wasn't really meant to be」；b. 更可操作的那一级：Can you reduce the project scope to the parts that "want" to work?
⇒ 而 b 配的故事很具体，也很值得照抄。 做让机器人听开放式语言指令（Can you clean up the trash but not the dishes?），初步有苗头；然后他们又加上「指令含糊时让机器人反问」等一堆想法 —— 结果 things weren't really working，又花了几个月。

⇒ 最后的做法是：回头问「哪些部分是真的能跑的」，把不会跑的那些砍掉、只保留方法本来就能处理的交互，而砍掉的部分写成论文的 limitations。 原话：「we rescoped the project to remove the hard parts that we didn't know how to solve yet… We described it as limitations in the paper」。⇒ 讲者的总结：「scoping down the project, especially if you scoped it up a little bit too eagerly, can also be a useful strategy」。

⚠️ p44 的转向有一个很漂亮的心理学技巧，而它的价值在于把一个模糊的决策变成了具体的。 先说问题：Often considered later than it should be considered! ＋ "sunk cost fallacy"。⇒ 讲稿把沉没成本这条说得更准：人很自然会想「我在这上面花了很多时间，所以以后花的时间会更少」—— 这是谬误，而且你实际的进展可能配不上你花掉的时间。
⇒ 而真正卡住人的是决策的形式：「继续做当前项目」vs「换去开一个新项目」 —— 而后者 is a super nebulous thing! ⇒ 「换一个新项目」可以指任何东西，所以你是在拿一个具体的东西和一片虚无比较，而那种比较没法做，只会让人焦虑。
⇒ 解法是换一个问法：Advice: spend time thinking about other research projects! 然后把决策改成 「继续当前项目」vs「做项目 B」vs「做项目 C」vs … ⇒ 幻灯的评价带了个笑脸：This decision is a lot more straightforward, less anxiety inducing! 🥳
⇒ 这一招的一般形式值得记住：当一个决策难做，先检查是不是因为其中一个选项太模糊 —— 把它具体化，决策本身就变容易了。 ⚠ 而它有一个前提条件，就是幻灯那句 spend time thinking about other research projects：你必须平时就在想别的项目，否则到了要转向的时候，手上没有 B 和 C 可比。⇒ 换句话说，这个技巧要提前付成本。

notes.say:
原话（为什么「先搭基础设施」是陷阱）：“wherever possible, it's good to front load the risk in the project. Think about, what is the reason why this might not succeed? And before developing infrastructure, before coding up the entire algorithm and so forth, if you can formulate and run simple experiments that test the core unknowns that you have, then you can bring the risk to the beginning of the project. And this can be really uncomfortable. Because oftentimes, building the infrastructure, coding the algorithm, whatever, that's like the easy part. That's the part where you can seemingly make some progress on the project. But if you do all that and then, at the end, realize that the core unknown actually ended up not working out, then you wasted all of that time—— even though it seemingly seemed like progress.”

原话（两个把风险前置的具体例子）：“I worked on meta learning in the past. And the goal was to see if you can quickly adapt with a very small amount of data… But actually, designing a meta learning system on a real robot is a ton of work… And so what I did is I first set up an experiment where the tasks—— instead of learning robot tasks, the tasks were regressing to simple 1D sinusoid curves. So really, really simple problem. And then just tested, can you learn with a few data points, like five data points, to regress to the curve? And so it was this experiment that I coded up in a day… Another example… I've been thinking a little bit about how to get robots to follow different kinds of language instructions, including language instructions for different strategies. And there's a couple of risks for this. One is getting good labels for the strategies. And the second is actually getting the robot to pay attention to those different strategies. And that second one actually seemed like the bigger challenge. And I took a data set where it was like a really, really simple problem, where in some of the data, the robot used the right gripper. And in some of the data, the robot used the left gripper. And then I trained a policy just to see if it could do that very simple thing, very easy to evaluate, and I could automatically determine if it was using the right or left from the data rather than doing labeling.”

原话（简化那个故事，以及那个「连单任务都不行」的转折）：“at one point, I was trying to train robots to be able to see a video of a human doing a task and then do the task themselves with imitation learning. Collected a really diverse data set of robot demonstrations and then asked a human to do what the robot did of all sorts of tasks. And we just told people collecting the data, do whatever you want. Do lots of things. Nothing worked when training on this data. Spent like months trying to get the robot to do it. And then what we did is we simplified to just a single task setting. Like, can we get the robot to do one task and make sure our imitation learning stack works? It actually didn't work. And so we had to debug that, get it to work on one task, then get it to work on three tasks, then get it to work on 10 tasks.”

原话（把项目砍回「它愿意成」的那部分）：“despite having positive initial signs of life, after we introduced all those ideas, things weren't really working. And we kind of tried all sorts of—— we spent a couple of months trying to get it to work. And at some point, we kind of went back and thought about, well, OK, it was working before. What parts of this thing do work? And what parts of these things are harder to work with our current method? And then we rescoped the project to remove the hard parts that we didn't know how to solve yet and to only consider the kind of interactions that our method did work with… We described it as limitations in the paper. And so scoping down the project, especially if you scoped it up a little bit too eagerly, can also be a useful strategy.”

原话（转向：把「换个新项目」换成「做项目 B 还是 C」）：“deciding when to pivot is really hard because you're often thinking about, should I continue working on my current project? Or should I switch to starting a new project? And this option of switching to a new project is really nebulous. This could mean a lot of different things.… And so one kind of mental trick for thinking about this sort of decision about whether to pivot is to change this decision and actually spend time thinking about other projects that you would do and then try to formulate the decision as continuing working on the current project versus working on project B or working on project C and so forth. And this decision is much more concrete, a lot more straightforward to think about, less anxiety inducing.”

res.v:
⚠️ 这三页对你的用处最直接，而且第一条是一个该在本周做完的实验。
按 p42：在搭基础设施之前，先用最快的方式测核心未知数。而你的核心未知数已经很清楚了：节点级档位分配，到底比「整条工作流统一一档」好多少？
⇒ 而那两个例子给了你照抄的形状：保留核心未知数，去掉全部工程量。
⇒ 所以你的「正弦曲线实验」应该长这样：取一个工作流、一个数据集的 200 条 query，穷举所有节点的档位组合（3 个节点 × 2 档 = 8 种；5 个节点就抽样），全部真跑一遍，然后直接算三个数：
① 最好的逐 query 节点级配置的 G（事后最优，这是上界）；② 最好的单一全局配置的 G（工作流级最优）；③ 二者之差。⇒ 那个差就是你整篇论文的空间。而这个实验不需要任何学习、不需要任何框架 —— 一个脚本、一个下午、几十美元的 API 费。
⇒ 如果差很小（比如 2%），那按 p42 第 4 条，你现在就该知道，而不是在搭完框架之后才知道。 ⇒ 而且那也不是坏消息：它会把你推向一个更好的问题（比如「怎么为每个工作流选一个全局配置」—— 更简单、也许更有用）。⇒ 这正是「不要在核心未知数有活的迹象之前，心理上认定这就是我的项目」。
⇒ 顺带注意例二里那个最妙的细节，它对你有一个直接的对应：她把「左右手」这个可以从数据里自动判定的属性当成标签，从而把「标注」这个次要风险也绕开了。 ⇒ 你的对应是：第一阶段的「理想档位」标签可以完全自动算出来（跑一遍、对答案），不需要任何人工。⇒ 这意味着你的核心实验没有标注瓶颈 —— 这是一个真实的便宜，值得在论文里点一句。
⚠️ p43 那个「连单任务都不行」的转折，对你是一条具体的执行顺序建议。
他们花了几个月在多任务上，而毛病在最基础那层。⇒ 你的对应基础层是什么？「在一个节点上，给定档位，我能可靠地判定它的输出对不对吗？」
⇒ 这件事听起来太基础，但它正是会出问题的地方：中间节点的输出往往没有标准答案（只有最终答案有）。 ⇒ 所以在做任何路由之前，先确认：你的 Acc 信号是挂在最终输出上的，那么单个节点的「对不对」你其实测不到。⇒ 这会直接影响你第一阶段的设计（只能做端到端的信用分配，不能做逐节点的直接监督）。⇒ 先把这件事想透，否则你会在一个测不到的量上建方法。
⇒ 而 p43 第 5 条（砍回「它愿意成」的那部分）给了你一条预备方案，建议现在就想好：如果逐 query 的节点级太难，退到「按任务类型的节点级」（同一类任务共用一套节点档位配置）。⇒ 这保留了「节点级」这个核心卖点，去掉了「逐 query 预测」这个最难的部分，而且砍掉的那部分正好写成 limitations —— 讲者那个故事就是这么做的。
⚠ 最后 p44 那个转向技巧对你有一个需要现在付成本的含义：你必须平时就在想别的项目，否则到了该转向的时候，手上没有 B 和 C 可比。 ⇒ 具体建议：维护一个「候选项目」的小清单，每条只写两行（问题是什么 + 路子是什么）。⇒ 这门课的 L18 前半那七个开放问题就是现成的素材来源，而 p27 第一问（离线指标）已经是你的 A，p15 第 1 问（大规模准确的价值函数）和 p19 第 2 问（边探索边保持安全）都可以当 B 和 C 记下来。

29.q: p32 三条现实里，第一条是什么？而讲者说它在整套方法论里扮演什么角色？
o: 研究需要大量算力；所以要选能复现的题
研究需要导师指导；所以要选有人带的方向
研究周期很长；所以要尽早发表
不到 1% 的研究想法有持久影响（很多想法连论文都变不成，变成论文的也多半影响很小）；而它是后面整套方法论的前提 ——「a lot of what I'll say has to do with dealing with that sort of risk」
29.why: ⇒ 所以 p42 那套「把风险前置、多试、晚承诺」之所以是对的，正是因为这个 1% —— 两处要连起来读，否则 p42 看起来只是一堆技巧。讲稿里她直接放了自己一堆想法的结局：「here are the outcomes of some of my research ideas. And here are the outcome of some more of my research ideas. And there's a lot of failure」。

29.q: 「简单的想法影响更大」，理由是什么？
o: 简单的想法更容易被审稿人接受
简单的想法训练成本更低
简单的想法更容易证明
因为在一个规模说话的时代，只有简单的东西能被 scale、容易被集成进不同系统、容易让别人在上面接着做 —— 而影响力来自被用上
29.why: ⇒ 实际含义：「我的算法很精巧」常常是缺点而不是优点。一个要五个超参、三个阶段、两个辅助损失才跑得动的方法，即使在你的实验里更好，也很难被别人用上。而第二条现实（研究是增量的）的例子是 AlphaFold —— 它自己也站在 CASP 那个二十年的学术项目和神经网络的进展上。

29.q: 讲者给「失败的项目也有用」提了一个具体理由（不是安慰话）。是什么？
o: 失败能锻炼研究能力
它让别人能在上面接着做，或者让别人能排除掉已经试过的想法 ——「这条路我们试过了，不行」本身是一个对社群有价值的产出
失败能帮助找到真正的兴趣
失败的项目可以改投别的会议
29.why: ⇒ 这也接到了 p46 那句「就算效果不好也值得分享」。另外 p33 大纲有一个刻意的旁注：first three are equally important!（挑什么做 · 怎么做 · 怎么分享）——「it's easy to think that maybe number 2 is the most important… But all of these are actually really, really important」。而把「分享」提到同等地位的理由在 p46：研究的产出是知识，知识没人知道就等于没有产出。

34.q: 一个研究项目要同时有「重要的问题」和「接近它的路子」。幻灯用哪两个反例说明？
o: 证明一个新界 / 做一个新数据集
「解决气候变化」缺路子（重要但明天不知道写哪行代码）· 「一个让机器人成功率涨 1% 的精巧算法」缺问题（有路子但天花板太低）
做一个新基准 / 复现一篇论文
训一个更大的模型 / 调一组更好的超参
34.why: ⚠ 注意幻灯刻意写了 1%：它不是说那个算法没用，而是说它的上限太低。而 Step 1 就是用来检查上限的：假设一切顺利、实验全部成功，那时候的结论是什么？那个结论重要吗？讲稿更锋利的问法：「what is the upper bound of that project? And if the upper bound is not very high, then usually it doesn't make for a very good project」。

34.q: Step 3 的措辞里有一个关键的转折。它问的到底是什么？
o: 把所有你能想到的失败理由「残酷诚实」地摆上桌之后，它还有多大机会成 —— 如果没有，那它多半不会成
这个想法需要多少资源
这个想法别人做过没有
这个想法有多大机会成功
34.why: 理由又回到那个 1%：「that's mostly just because of the reality of most ideas not actually working in research」。⇒ 换句话说：基础概率已经很低了，所以你不该在还有已知的大风险时就乐观。而 Step 2（你对它兴奋吗）之所以是判据而不只是鼓励，也和这个 1% 配套：既然多数想法会失败，那你需要的是能撑过失败的动力。

34.q: p37 里，讲者为什么偏向「问题驱动」？最锋利的那个理由是什么？
o: 问题驱动更容易找到合作者
问题驱动的论文更容易发表
因为想法可能「不想成」（the idea just doesn't want to work）—— 如果你的目标是「让这个想法成」，那想法不成你就被困住了；而目标是「解掉问题」时，换个想法只是换条路，项目还活着
问题驱动需要的背景知识更少
34.why: 还有一层更容易被忽略的：从想法出发时，就算它确实解了某个问题，也可能存在更好的解法 —— 那这个想法就没多少影响力。问题驱动的已知坏处幻灯也写了：May be harder to write paper if solution is obvious in retrospect；但好处是一句带笑脸的话：But guaranteed to be working on an important problem :)

38.q: 「先找瓶颈」这一招的要点是什么？
o: 如果问题卡在数据上，而你去研究算法，那你多半只能看到几个百分点 —— 因为大的性能提升在数据那一侧
先找最难的技术环节攻克
先找算力最省的方案
先找已有开源实现的环节
38.why: ⇒ 这和 Step 1 是同一件事的两种问法：「上限有多高」问终点，「瓶颈在哪」问为什么现在到不了终点 —— 而后者更可操作，它直接告诉你该动哪里。而这招还能用在很长远的目标上（让 LLM 证 P vs NP、让机器人在陌生厨房做一碗麦片）：单个项目都解不了，但可以问「到那里的瓶颈是什么」，然后在下一个项目里做那一段。

38.q: p39 那个故事里，她为什么能在一个自己不擅长的方向上做出 1300 引用的工作？
o: 因为当时没多少人在做，而原因是「大家没意识到这些模型有多差」 —— 她从机器人那个方向走过来，所以看到了做视觉的人看不到的问题
她有 Google 的算力支持
因为她找到了更好的架构
因为视频生成当时是热门方向
38.why: ⇒ 这是整个故事的机制：她之所以有机会，正是因为从另一个方向走过来、因而看到了别人看不到的问题。做视觉的人不知道这些模型在机器人上有多不够用，因为他们不拿它做控制。⚠ 而她对自己的评估很诚实：「I wasn't necessarily the best person to do this. I had never built a generative model before.」⇒ Takeaway: Don't box yourself into one area.

38.q: 「别做完美主义者」的理由，讲稿补的那半句是什么？
o: 审稿人并不要求完美
完美的项目通常已经有人做了
时间有限，不可能样样做好
你在一开始永远不可能知道一个项目的影响力 ——「否则它就不是研究了」；所以「挑一个完美的项目」在定义上就做不到，你得在某个点上直接开始试
38.why: ⇒ 把 p38–p40 三页并起来，它们在反对同一种行为：在动手之前过度优化选择。瓶颈那条说「别在错的地方使劲」，故事那条说「别因为领域标签就放弃一条路」，完美主义那条说「别为了选对而迟迟不开始」。⇒ 合起来的姿态是：想清楚该往哪使劲，然后尽快开始，并且不介意绕路。

41.q: 「把风险前置」为什么让人不舒服？讲者给的理由很诚实。
o: 因为导师通常要求先搭框架
因为早期实验容易失败，打击信心
因为搭基础设施、把算法写出来常常是「容易的部分」，也是「看起来在进步」的那部分 —— 而先去面对那个可能毁掉整个项目的未知数，让人不舒服
因为早期没有足够的数据
41.why: 后果说得很直接：「if you do all that and then realize that the core unknown ended up not working out, then you wasted all of that time—— even though it seemingly seemed like progress」。所以幻灯那句 This is uncomfortable!! 不是在说实验难做，而是在说面对那个问题本身让人不舒服。

41.q: 那两个「把风险前置」的例子有一个共同形状。是什么？
o: 都用更小的模型先试
把真实任务换成一个保留了核心未知数、但去掉了全部工程量的玩具任务 —— 正弦曲线保留「少样本快速适应」去掉机器人；左右手保留「策略能不能被语言区分」去掉标注和复杂指令
都在仿真里先跑一遍
都先复现一篇已有论文
41.why: 元学习那个「用五个点回归一维正弦曲线」的实验，她一天就写完了。而左右手那个例子最妙的一笔是：左右手可以从数据里自动判定、不用标注 —— 这样就把「标签」这个次要风险也绕开了，只留下她要测的那一个。第 4 条是这几条的收口：Don't mentally commit to project before signs of life on core unknown —— 关键词是 mentally 和 signs of life。

41.q: p43 那个「看人做一遍再自己做」的故事，关键转折是什么？
o: 他们换了更好的模仿学习算法
他们最终改用了强化学习
他们在多任务上卡了几个月，简化到单任务去验证管线时发现 —— 连单任务也不行；调通之后才 1 个 → 3 个 → 10 个
他们发现数据采集的指令太含糊
41.why: ⇒ 要点：他们花了几个月在一个多任务问题上，而真正的毛病在最基础的那一层。如果一开始就先跑通单任务，那几个月就省下来了。⇒ 所以「简化」不只是调试手段，它是一个定序原则：先确认地基，再往上加。

41.q: p44 那个关于「什么时候转向」的心理学技巧是什么？
o: 把决策从「继续当前项目 vs 换去开一个新项目」（后者太模糊，等于拿具体的东西和一片虚无比）改成「继续当前项目 vs 做项目 B vs 做项目 C」 —— 具体得多，也不那么让人焦虑
先把当前项目写成论文再说
给项目设一个固定的时间上限
请导师替你决定
41.why:
⇒ 一般形式值得记住：当一个决策难做，先检查是不是因为其中一个选项太模糊 —— 把它具体化，决策本身就变容易了。⚠ 而它有一个前提，就是幻灯那句 spend time thinking about other research projects：你必须平时就在想别的项目，否则到了要转向的时候手上没有 B 和 C 可比 —— 这个技巧要提前付成本。
沉没成本那条讲稿说得更准：人很自然会想「我在这上面花了很多时间，所以以后花的时间会更少」—— 这是谬误，而且你实际的进展可能配不上你花掉的时间。

41.q: p43 第 5 条「它想不想成」的第二级（更可操作的那一级）是什么？
o: 能不能把项目范围砍回「它愿意成」的那部分？ —— 讲者的故事里，他们把加上去的难部分砍掉、只保留方法本来就能处理的交互，而砍掉的部分写成了论文的 limitations
降低实验的评估标准
找更多人一起做
换一个更简单的算法试试
41.why: 讲者的总结：「scoping down the project, especially if you scoped it up a little bit too eagerly, can also be a useful strategy」。而第一级是：如果它完全不想成，那它很可能没什么影响力 ——「if someone else is trying to get it to work and it also doesn't really work for them, then maybe the idea just wasn't really meant to be」。
